fieldDescription: When and how fast the Threat spreads. The incursion begins only after the vanilla abyss story flags fire (finding the Onslaught Mk.I or encountering the Threat).
Master switch. Turning this off freezes the incursion entirely (existing colonies remain).
The swarm was always coming: skip all triggers and begin the incursion immediately in a new game (takes effect on existing saves too). The story triggers below are ignored while this is on.

Alternate start trigger: a player colony reaching the size below wakes the swarm even without touching the abyss questline - whichever comes first. A maxed colony is exactly the concentration of technology the Threat exists to destroy.
Player colony size that wakes the swarm (6 = vanilla max via natural growth).
How often the incursion clock advances. Higher = slower everything.

The incursion begins from one resource-complete OG home system (its full mining/refining/forge chain is founded at once from the Abyss). Values above 1 add that many extra single-colony fringe footholds beyond the OG.
Days a seeded system incubates before a Seeding Swarm is dispatched to found a fabrication colony there.
Hard cap on simultaneously infested systems.
Minimum colony size before it can dispatch colonization waves.

The swarm founds real colonies that grow from size 1 and run a genuinely self-contained hive economy: their mining worlds feed refineries feed forge worlds that build the ships. Shortages of metals or machinery stall growth; hull shortages shrink garrisons and strikes. Cut supply lines and destroy link colonies to starve the network.

Days per size level, multiplied by current size (a size-5 colony takes 300 days to reach 6). Growth is paced by colony health: shortages slow it sharply, and a colony in outright decline loses population instead.
Size cap for Threat colonies.

Spare copies of each production link (refinery, forge, fuel plant) the hive builds as it spreads - one per infested system it holds, up to this many. Under vanilla's economy one producer feeds every hive world that can reach it, so spares add nothing until the original is lost; they exist so that cutting the hive's supply of anything means cutting several worlds. 1 = a single point of failure for each.
Escort strength of colonization fleets: 0 = none, 1 = light, 2 = medium, 3 = heavy.

Days between replacement Defense Swarms fabricating at a colony. This is the hive's whole military tempo: expeditions are mustered FROM the garrison, so this paces strikes and colonization waves too. Killing swarms delays everything until the nexus regrows them - one fleet at a time.

Colonies cover each other: a worn-down colony's garrison is topped up by Defense Swarms sent from the best-covered colony that can reach it - same system first, then any system within the donor's fuel range - until garrisons balance out. The swarms physically fly there and can be intercepted en route. A donor must be able to regrow what it sends (Fabrication Core and Swarm Nexus both up) and always keeps one swarm home. To strip a colony bare you must outpace every colony that can reach it, or cut the fuel range that connects them.
How many Defense Swarms the hive may dispatch as reinforcements per colony poll (about half a day). Higher means help arrives in bigger, faster bursts; 1 is a slow trickle.

A garrison slot is a promise of a certain weight of defense. A Defense Swarm shot below this fraction of the fleet points it was fabricated with - or one of a lower tier than the slot wants, such as a small colony's swarm sent to reinforce a big one - is a weak holder: it keeps fighting, but no longer blocks the Swarm Nexus, which grows a proper replacement at its normal respawn cadence and recycles the weak swarm. Lower = damaged swarms hold their slot longer; higher = the hive replaces battle damage sooner.

If on, colony growth is paced by economic health: shortages of core production inputs (ore, metals, volatiles, rare ore/metals) slow and then stop growth until the hive economy recovers. Structure disruption and severe shortages can push a colony into outright decline regardless of this setting.

The first hive system carries Domain-era items, as a swarm out of the Abyss would: a Pristine Nanoforge on its largest forge, and a Mantle Bore, Plasma Dynamo, Catalytic Core or Synchrotron wherever its own deposits leave a production link short. Vanilla's chain only balances at size 8 with these - a plain forge makes 6 hulls against a Swarm Nexus wanting 8, a Pristine one makes 9. Every later colony draws on the home hive, so the items lift the whole swarm, and they are the loot for taking it. Applies to existing saves on the next tick.

Chance that any forge outside the home system's Pristine one carries a Corrupted Nanoforge (plus 1 hull, plus 20 percent quality). A fixed roll per world, so the answer never changes from month to month and a rebuilt forge keeps its luck. 0 disables.

The hive is a closed economy that never trades with the Core worlds, so vanilla's distance-from-Core accessibility penalty models a supply line it doesn't have. This cancels that penalty for hive colonies: 1 removes it fully, 0 leaves vanilla behavior (fringe seeds far from the Core then import almost nothing and stall). Distance from the rest of the hive does not move accessibility either way - vanilla's same-faction proximity term is only ever a bonus.

Shipping units (in and out) a hive world keeps while its Megaport or Spaceport is disrupted. Vanilla keeps a disrupted port counted as present and same-faction shipping never falls below 5 units, so on its own a disrupted hive port changes nothing. At the default 3 a mature world's factories run on a trickle - a size-8 forge gets 3 of the 8 metals it wants - growth stalls, fuel reach shrinks, and its own output reaches the rest of the hive only as that trickle. Kept above zero on purpose: with the Fabrication Core also down, machinery is imported, and zero shipping made a port cut deadlier than a Core cut. 0 = nothing docks at all; -1 = leave vanilla behavior.
If on, worlds decivilized by Threat bombardment become colonization targets - the swarm moves into the graveyards it creates, even inside inhabited systems.

From phase 3, the colonial defense boards offer missions against specific hive infrastructure (rare mining, fuel, refining, swarm nexus) - ordinary contracts that arrive over the comm network and must be accepted before they expire, each explaining what cutting that link does to the swarm. Several offers stand at once, ranked by network impact against difficulty, and the weakest is withdrawn when a more valuable target comes online. Accept one and the completion clock starts. Disruption pays half, decivilization pays full; failing or abandoning costs reputation with the sponsoring faction.
Payout per target colony size (a size-6 hive world pays 6x this for destruction, half for disruption).
How long an offer stays posted before it is withdrawn unaccepted. Real days - deliberately NOT compressed by the debug fast clock.

Days you have to complete a contract once you accept it. Real days - deliberately NOT compressed by the debug fast clock, since this is your window to act. Missing the deadline is a mission failure and costs reputation with the sponsor.

How many contracts the defense boards keep offered at once. Accepted contracts do not count - take all three and the board refills. Offers on a lever already open are discounted when picking the next, so the list spreads across rare mining, fuel, refining and nexus rather than stacking on one.

How much better a new objective must score than the weakest offered one before it displaces it - 1.35 means it must score a third higher again. Lower values make the board churn more aggressively; 1.0 means any improvement triggers a swap. Accepted contracts are never displaced. Note LunaLib renders these descriptions through a text formatter, so avoid literal percent signs here.
Days a newly posted offer is guaranteed before it can be withdrawn for a better one - your window to decide. Offers are also never withdrawn while you are in the target's system.

How far a target's score is raised for sitting inside a faction navy's operating radius (a Patrol HQ, Military Base or High Command within Response Range). A hive world that has crept into defended space is the sector's immediate problem, and is cheaper to kill besides - task forces grind its garrison and a purge expedition may finish it, which still completes your contract in full. 0 ignores faction proximity entirely.

Reward premium on the strategic (expensive) tier over the immediate (cheap) tier. The strategic board names the decisive target regardless of what taking it costs, so it pays more for the same colony size.

Phases are capability, not calendar. Phase 1: fringe expansion (no attacks). Phase 2: begins when some colony can actually stage a strike (strike-sized, forged, fueled). Phase 3: core worlds in reach once some colony can field a full-budget armada (size 6+ with a near-nominal hull economy). Burn forges, cut fuel, or shrink colonies and the phase genuinely regresses.
If on, phase 3 eventually puts the core worlds (size 6+ colonies) in reach.
Large Threat colonies launch incursion fleets at inhabited worlds - real fleets you can intercept and fight alongside the defenders. Worlds they decivilize may be converted into new hive colonies.
Sector-wide cap on simultaneous Threat strikes. 0 = unlimited: every hive system with the means keeps a strike in flight.

Light-years of reach per unit of fuel an expedition carries - one rule for everyone. Reach = this x the smaller of fuel available at the launching colony and the fuel its fleets can carry (the tier settings below times vanilla's fleet-size figure for the colony). Hive strikes and seeding waves range from their staging colony by it; faction task forces and siege expeditions, and your own commissioned expeditions, range from their military world by it. A colony with no fuel sends nothing.

Fuel units an expedition carries at a fleet-size figure of 100 percent. Faction and player worlds use vanilla's own fleet-size figure untouched - colony size, doctrine, hull shortage, stability, alpha core, skills, the Fleets percentage on the colony screen - so a 300 percent world carries 12 and is bound by fuel instead. Hive worlds use hive vitality x size / 4: a healthy size-4 hive lifts a full load (20 light-years at the defaults), size 8 twice that, a size-2 foothold half, and a besieged world less as its vitality falls. All the fuel in the sector is no use to a colony that only fields small fleets.
Minimum colony size before it launches strikes (replaces the old 'saturated' stage).

Scales how heavily each mustered Defense Swarm is re-embodied as an expedition fleet. Strikes are drawn from the colony's REAL garrison (everything above its defensive reserve, only at full strength), so their size is fundamentally set by the garrison the colony fields - this multiplier just up- or down-tiers the fleets.
Minimum days between strikes that target YOUR colonies specifically. NPC worlds get no such mercy.

If on, an incursion still PREPARING at its staging colony is stillborn when that colony's forge is broken: raid the forge into disruption, bombard the colony, or destroy it before the fleets depart. Once an expedition departs it is autonomous and cannot be recalled.

If on, Threat strikes may target story-critical worlds and decivilize them outright (the engine normally refuses the killing blow). WARNING: erasing quest worlds can permanently break unfinished vanilla storylines. If off, strikes never target story-critical worlds at all.

Overall scale on hive ground-defense strength. This is the input to raid effectiveness AND the base of the bombardment fuel bill, so it scales both how costly marines are and how costly fuel is. Hive defenses keep firing at half effect while disrupted, so repeat passes are never near-free.

Every hive lives deep underground behind ground defenses anchored to colony size (400 points per size by default, immune to unrest, multiplied by the defense industries - a mature hive's true figure runs into the thousands). Bombardment can NEVER reduce a hive's population: saturation costs the full defense figure for days of disruption, tactical costs a fraction and suppresses the war-strata longer, marines cut deepest. The only way a hive dies is decline - its population falling to size 1 under sustained disruption or shortages.

Flat ground-defense points per colony size, before industry multipliers (a size-4 hive fields a 1600-point base, size-8 fields 3200; ground defenses, heavy batteries and the nexus multiply it further). This is the number bombardment fuel costs are priced from, and it drives marine raid effectiveness and casualties. Hive defenses ignore unrest - the machines do not riot.
Defense multiplier bonus from the hive Ground Defenses structure: mult = 1 + bonus (x2 at the default 1.0). Scaled down by machinery/metals shortages.
Defense multiplier bonus from hive Heavy Batteries: mult = 1 + bonus (x3 at the default 2.0). Scaled down by machinery/metals shortages.
Defense multiplier bonus from the Swarm Nexus: mult = 1 + bonus (x1.5 at the default 0.5).

Fraction of a defense structure's bonus that keeps working the moment it is disrupted - machines do not rout. From there it wears down (see Defense Wear Days). At 0 disrupted structures contribute nothing at once (vanilla behavior, makes repeat bombardments cheap); at 1 a fresh disruption does not weaken defenses at all.

Disruption days on a structure's clock at which it has worn to nothing: a defense structure's surviving bonus, and a disrupted Core's or Nexus's fabrication factor, both fall in a straight line from their fresh-disruption value to zero at this many days. Disruption stacks with every tactical pass and every successful raid, so an organ carrying 300 days has been hit again and again - and by then it is scrap. At the defaults one tactical pass (60 days) leaves 40 percent of a battery's bonus firing, two raids on top about 25 percent; a Core carrying 150 days fabricates at half its Core-Down factor. The size-anchored base defense never wears, so bombardment gets cheaper as a siege grinds on but never free. 0 disables wear.
Scale on the saturation fuel bill. At 1.0 saturation costs exactly the colony's ground-defense strength.
Tactical bombardment fuel cost as a fraction of the colony's ground-defense strength - concentrated fire on exposed military targets is far cheaper than saturating the world.
Days of disruption a saturation pass inflicts on a hive's industries (vanilla is 365 - the hive's deep strata reknit almost immediately).

Days of disruption a tactical pass inflicts on the hive's war-strata (ground defenses, batteries, nexus). Longer than saturation - concentrated fire on exposed military targets is the efficient way to suppress defenses.
Multiplier on marine casualties when raiding hive worlds - the counter-swarms contest every corridor.

NPC purge doctrine: an AI siege expedition keeps delivering tactical bombardments - whose disruption now stacks, wearing the war-strata further with each pass - while any defense structure's surviving effect is still above this fraction. Once bombed below it, the expedition lands troops instead. At 0.5 the expedition makes a single softening pass then raids (the old behavior); lower values buy more bombardment passes before the ground assault; 0 grinds the war-strata to nothing first.

A persistent army: land marines and heavy armaments on a hive world (Ground operations, on the military options menu) and they stay, fighting after you break orbit. The front burns heavy armaments as upkeep - the stockpile is its supply countdown - and marines attrit at flat daily rates, faster once the armaments run dry. Strong enough (against the world's current, worn defense figure) it HOLDS - suppressing the hive's organs and able to push the stratum campaign below; weaker it GRINDS only the outer defenses until they wear down; weaker still it is a mere foothold. Resupply and withdraw by docking; live Defense Swarms in orbit block that, so the hive's reinforcement network is the counter-siege.
Master switch for the ground-front mechanic. Existing fronts keep ticking if turned off mid-siege; the deploy option is hidden.

Effective strength (marines times entrenchment) as a fraction of the colony's current ground-defense figure needed to HOLD - suppressing the Fabrication Core, Swarm Nexus, port and both defense structures. 0.25 mirrors vanilla's own raid-disruption threshold. The defense figure is the worn, current one, so softening the world first (tactical passes, raids) lowers the bar, and a holding front keeps lowering it.

Fraction of the defense figure needed to GRIND: too weak to reach the deep organs, the front harasses the Ground Defenses and Heavy Batteries at the reduced rate below. As they wear, the hold requirement falls and the front upgrades itself - the path from an early landing to a full siege.

Days added to each suppressed structure's disruption clock per day held. The clock counts down one day per day naturally, so 2.0 nets +1 day of accumulated wear per day - and the clock is the same wear mechanic raids and bombardments feed (see Disruption Wear Days).
Suppression-rate multiplier while only grinding the defense structures.
Fraction of the front's current marines lost per 30 days while supplied - the hive contests the ground forever, so a siege is never free.
Attrition multiplier once the front's heavy armaments run out.
Heavy armaments the front consumes per colony size per 30 days (size 6 = 2 per day at the default). What the front has on hand is exactly how long it lasts unsupplied - legible and plannable.
Days of digging in to reach the full entrenchment multiplier below. Rewards sustained sieges over drive-by landings.
Effectiveness multiplier of a fully entrenched front (1.0 = entrenchment does nothing).
Marines below which the front is overrun outright.

If on, a tactical bombardment with your own front deployed costs it marines (fraction below) - and in exchange the ground forces mark targets, so the strike's disruption also lands on the Fabrication Core and port, not just the war-strata.
Fraction of the front's marines lost to each danger-close tactical pass.

Days after a saturation bombardment during which ground forces cannot land - the surface is a radiological ruin. Keep this at or above the saturation disruption duration, or sat bombing becomes the best siege opener instead of a tradeoff (its role is silencing a world, at the price of ground tempo).

A size-S hive is S strata deep with the Fabrication Core at the center - and ERADICATION IS A GROUND VICTORY, the only way a hive dies. A front strong enough to hold can be ordered to push: each stratum taken strips its share of the base defenses and of the hive's output, and taking the last one destroys the Core and the colony. After each stratum the front consolidates at a checkpoint, requests reinforcement, and - given no orders within the window - pushes on by doctrine; you can instead order it to entrench and stand fast, or pull it out (which requires controlling the space over the planet). The hive counter-attacks on a cadence paced by its health: starving its economy is what makes those counter-attacks rare and feeble. NPC expeditions land their own fronts and run the same campaign.

Base days one stratum push takes at even strength; scaled by the defense-to-strength ratio (clamped 0.5x to 3x), so an overwhelming front advances in days and a marginal one crawls. As strata fall and strip base defense, later pushes genuinely get faster.
Fraction of the front's marines lost per 30 days while assaulting (replaces the entrenched attrition rate for the duration). Pushing is how you win and how you bleed.
Heavy-armaments burn multiplier while assaulting - offensives eat materiel.
Effectiveness multiplier of a front whose heavy armaments have run out - marines without materiel fight at this fraction of their strength, on top of the raised attrition. Resupply before pushing.
Defense multiplier of a dug-in (non-pushing) front against hive counter-attacks. A front caught mid-assault defends without it.
Days a front consolidates after taking a stratum, requesting reinforcement and awaiting orders. Told nothing, it pushes on by doctrine; order it to entrench to stop the advance.

Base days between hive counter-attacks against a front, DIVIDED by the colony's health - a starved colony at 25 percent health attacks four times more rarely. A counter-attack that beats the front's (entrenchment-boosted) strength retakes a held stratum and costs marines; one that doubles a stratum-less beachhead destroys it.
Fraction of the front's marines lost to a counter-attack it fails to repel.
Days of heavy-armaments supply an NPC expedition's ground landing carries. When it runs dry the front withers; the next expedition lands a fresh one.

NPC factions behave exactly as vanilla until the Threat strikes one of their colonies - that strike puts the faction in WAR MODE. A mobilised faction's colonies accrue visible reserves of marines, heavy armaments, fuel and supplies, each from the colony's own production of the matching commodity, and every expedition draws its landing force and provisions from the colony it sails from - troops that ride the fleets as real cargo. Colonies ship stock to those staging bases by convoy: real fleets, interceptable, lootable. Your own faction mobilises the same way when the swarm first strikes a world of yours.
Master switch for war mode, per-colony reserves, convoys and fleet orders. Off, expeditions raise abstract troops as before.
Days after its last strike a mobilised faction stands down - only if no live hive remains in expedition range of its military worlds. Reserves are kept, frozen. 0 = mobilised for good.
Reserve marines a colony accrues per unit of its vanilla marine production (Patrol HQ, Military Base, High Command) per 30 days. A size-6 Military Base makes about 6 units.
Reserve heavy armaments per unit of the colony's hand-weapon production (Heavy Industry, Orbital Works) per 30 days.
Reserve fuel per unit of the colony's fuel production per 30 days.
Reserve supplies per unit of the colony's supply production per 30 days.
A colony stockpiles at most this many months of its own production of each commodity.
Months of its own production each colony holds the moment its faction mobilises - the peacetime depots the first sortie draws from. 0 starts every reserve empty.
Expeditions and sorties never draw a colony below this fraction of its cap - the home garrison's stock. Keeps a small faction from emptying its depots on one sortie and going quiet.
Marines every colony raises per size per 30 days regardless of industry, so no colony sits permanently at zero.

Exponent on every ground-war strength ratio - push pace, push attrition, counter-attack losses and overruns. 1 is linear and legible; 2 is Lanchester's square law, where concentrating twice the marines pays four times over. Dialog quotes stay exact at any value.
An expedition waits - and its base keeps calling convoys - unless the base holds this fraction of the marines the landing needs. 0 sails with whatever is there.
Fuel an expedition or task force draws from its base per fleet point per light-year of distance. A cost, not a gate.
Supplies an expedition or task force draws from its base per fleet point. A cost, not a gate.
Troop-transport share of a cargo-carrying expedition fleet (vanilla composition multiplier). Too low and the marines drawn will not all fit - the remainder stays home.
Whether mobilised factions ship reserves between their colonies by convoy. Off, each staging base fights with what it makes itself.
Light-years a donor colony will ship to a staging base.
Marines one convoy carries at most (transports are sized to the load). Fewer, larger convoys lose a smaller share per attack - keep this high.
Units of armaments, fuel and supplies one convoy carries at most.
Combat fleet points every convoy sails with, before the cargo-value escort below.
Extra escort fleet points per 1,000 of cargo value (marines count 1 each, armaments 0.5, fuel and supplies 0.1). A rich convoy is a real fleet.
A base's shortfall, as a fraction of one convoy load, below which no convoy sails.
Convoys one faction dispatches per 30-day tick at most, its neediest bases first. Fewer, larger convoys are safer than many small ones.

Mobilised factions run supply convoys to their ground fronts (marines and heavy armaments from the nearest base's reserve) and withdrawal convoys for fronts that call for a pickup. Runs wait at the hive system's jump-point while Defense Swarms hold the orbit - a garrisoned hive strangles the front.
Days of heavy-armaments upkeep a supply run tops a front up to.
A supply run reinforces a front back toward this fraction of its peak marine strength.
Days a supply or withdrawal run waits at the jump-point for the orbit to clear before turning for home with its cargo.
Hive colonies near a convoy's route may detach one Defense Swarm to hunt it - the swarm's own commerce raiding, paid for with a thinner garrison while it is out.
Light-years from a convoy route's midpoint within which a hive colony may send a raider.
Chance each eligible hive colony (Defense Swarms above its reserve) detaches a raider at a passing convoy; the nearest rolls first and one raider is enough.
Days a raider hunts its convoy before turning for home.
Fraction of its own cap a donor colony keeps back for itself.
A staging base stocks this many expeditions' worth of each reserve.
Days after which a convoy that has not arrived is written off with its cargo.

The war board's faction view lets you command a mobilised navy from anywhere: guard a colony's orbit, stage materiel to it by convoy, hold a hive system's jump-point, send a siege expedition, recall a fleet. Your own faction takes orders once mobilised; an ally does once your standing with it is high enough. Every sortie is built at the nearest base and paid from that base's reserve.
Whether the faction view offers Guard, Stage, Intercept, Siege and Recall buttons.
Relationship with an allied mobilised faction (from -1 to 1; 0.5 is cooperative) at which its navy takes your orders.
Combat fleet points of a guard or intercept task force.
Days a guard task force holds a colony's orbit before returning to base.
Days an intercept task force holds a hive system's jump-point.

The swarm answers who hurts it. Every faction earns grudge for strata taken, hives eradicated and raids or tactical passes landed; the sum is the hive's alarm. Both are shown on the war board and fade monthly. Alarm speeds up Swarm Nexus fabrication - the hive's whole military tempo - grudge points its strikes at that faction's worlds, and a ground victory draws an immediate retaliation strike at the winner. No hidden scaling: the numbers are on the board.
Master switch for grudge, alarm and retaliation.
Grudge points a faction earns for each stratum its ground front takes.
Grudge points for destroying a hive's Fabrication Core.
Grudge points for a successful raid or tactical bombardment pass on a hive world.
Fraction of every grudge that fades per 30 days.
Swarm Nexus fabrication-speed bonus per point of alarm: at 0.05, alarm 10 means garrisons - and therefore strikes and expansion - come 1.5 times as fast.
The most alarm can multiply fabrication speed by.
Strike-target weight bonus per point of a faction's grudge: at 0.2, grudge 10 makes that faction's worlds three times as likely to be struck.
A ground victory draws an immediate strike at the winning faction from the nearest hive that can muster one - a strike it could have launched anyway, aimed now.

A mobilised faction's siege calls its allies: every other mobilised faction with a base in reach may answer with a task force holding the hive's jump-point so the siege lands under cover. Your Rally button on a hive row does the same for every ally that takes your orders, plus a siege from the best-supplied of them.
Whether sieges post calls that allied mobilised factions answer.
Days a call stays open for allies to answer.
Chance per 30-day tick that an eligible ally answers an open call with an Intercept task force.

A world the swarm held and lost is a world it will try to seed again. An outpost is a faction-styled orbital station over such a world - no market, no economy - that blocks re-seeding until it is destroyed. You pay credits; a mobilised faction pays supplies and fuel from its nearest base and fortifies purged worlds on its own.
Whether outposts can be built on purged worlds, by you (Outpost button on the faction view) and by mobilised factions.
1 orbital station, 2 battlestation, 3 star fortress - in the faction's own style.
What you pay for an outpost.
Supplies a mobilised faction's base pays for an outpost.
Fuel a mobilised faction's base pays for an outpost.
Chance per 30-day tick that a mobilised faction fortifies an open purged world within reach of a base that can pay.

A recalled fleet (or one whose order ran out) comes home on a tracked leg: everything still aboard - marines, armaments, cargo - goes back into the base's reserve, and this fraction of the fuel and supplies it drew at launch is refunded, scaled by its surviving strength. A fleet lost on the way returns nothing.

A hive colony's health is its input satisfaction times the functionality of its fabrication organs. Since the ground-war rework low health only ever WEAKENS: growth stalls, garrisons rebuild slowly, reach shrinks, and counter-attacks against ground forces come rarely and feebly - but no colony dies without a ground victory.

Colony health multiplier the moment the Fabrication Core is disrupted; it wears further with the disruption days on the Core's clock (see Disruption Wear Days), to zero fabrication at the wear limit. A dead Core cripples the colony's vitality - and with it every counter-attack its strata can mount.
Colony health at or below which growth stops entirely (without yet declining).
Colony health at or above which the colony grows at its full configured pace; growth ramps linearly between the stall and full-pace thresholds.

When a Threat strike targets an NPC colony, its faction musters a task force against the attacking colony's garrison. Nearby navies also launch siege expeditions - tactical bombardments and commando raids that suppress a hive's organs and push it into decline, including (rarely, with extra escorts) full assaults on defended colonies. You can commission the same expedition from your own military colonies, priced by flotilla size and distance.
If on, an NPC faction whose colony is struck sends a counter-task-force against the attacking colony's Defense Swarms (only if it has a military world within range).
Sector-wide cap on simultaneous faction task forces / purge expeditions. 0 = unlimited.
Smallest task force a responding faction sends (fleet difficulty 0-10 scale).
Largest task force a responding faction sends.
Higher = weaker task forces for the same faction military strength. Task force difficulty = min + factionStrength / this.

Siege expeditions, NPC and commissioned alike, are sized to the target's defenses: an industry raid only lands when the ground force is at least a third of the defender strength, so fleets are added until the estimated ground strength clears that with headroom. NPC ground strength is a quarter of crew capacity, which tracks fleet size - one difficulty point of fleet lands about this much (measured: 22 points landed 947). Lower it if raids keep being repulsed, raise it if sieges arrive absurdly large.

Cap on how many fleets a siege expedition grows to while sizing itself to the target's defenses. Sizing assumes the tactical pass has already suppressed the war-strata (about 60 percent of the intact figure): a size-8 hive behind Heavy Batteries then needs about 3,600 ground strength, which is 9 full-size fleets. When the cap still leaves the force short, the commission quote says so and NPC sieges settle for the tactical bombardment.

If on, NPC navies launch siege expeditions at Threat colonies: tactical bombardments and commando raids that suppress a hive's organs and push it into decline - they can genuinely wither and erase colonies without your help, though never by bombardment alone.
Minimum days between NPC purge expeditions against any one colony.

Hive colonies up to this size are besieged PREEMPTIVELY - navies in range suppress young footholds before they entrench, fighting through their Defense Swarms. Larger defended colonies can draw a full assault too (extra escorts, longer cooldown - see below). 0 disables preemptive sieges.

Cooldown multiplier for full NPC assaults on DEFENDED entrenched colonies (garrisoned, above the preemptive size). Higher = rarer; these expeditions sail with an extra escort fleet to fight through the Defense Swarms.

A WOUNDED colony (open decline meter, or Core/Nexus/port still disrupted) draws the next expedition on this short cooldown instead of the full purge interval - navies press an advantage, turning single visits into sustained campaigns. The decline meter also does not regrow while any key organ is disrupted.

If on, you can commission a purge expedition against an infested system from the intel screen, provided one of your colonies with a Patrol HQ, Military Base or High Command is within Response Range. The expedition uses your faction's doctrine and blueprints, runs the full siege playbook autonomously, and posts an after-action sitrep. You pay up front; no refunds.

Credits per fleet-difficulty point of the commissioned flotilla (a heavy 4-fleet expedition is ~36 points). The flotilla is sized to the job - bigger and better-defended hive systems need, and cost, more.
Credits per light-year between your commissioning colony and the target system.
Systems defended by a live Remnant Nexus resist infestation - the swarm must win a war of machines first. Purging the Remnant yourself clears the Threat's path.
If on, the spread cannot claim a system with a live Remnant Nexus without first destroying it in a machine war.
Per-attempt chance the swarm destroys a defending Remnant Nexus. Failures are retried on later spread attempts.
The Threat is a machine menace at war with all life. These control how that reads on the relations screen and whether the sector treats exterminating the swarm as a war crime.
